lead: Canonical LR(1) parsing removes a weakness of SLR. SLR decides a reduction by FOLLOW of the left-hand side, a set that is often too wide. An LR(1) item carries one lookahead terminal, so a reduction is allowed only when that exact terminal comes next. This extra detail lets the parser handle grammars that SLR rejects, such as assignment with pointers. Some syllabi call it CLR or canonical LR. Parser generators use the same idea, though many merge states to save space.
prereq: You need LR(0) items and closure, SLR tables, and FIRST sets from Unit 2.

sections.h3: The LR(1) item and its closure

blocks.text: An LR(1) item is a pair [A → α . β, a]. A → αβ is a production; the dot shows how much of the right side the parser has matched; a is one terminal called the lookahead. The item means: we are trying to complete A → αβ, and after A the next input symbol must be a. For example, [S → L . = R, $] says the parser has matched L, expects = next, and after the whole S the input must end ($).

Closure adds items until no new ones appear. If [A → α . B β, a] is in I and B → γ is a production, then for every terminal b in FIRST(β a) add [B → . γ, b]. FIRST(β a) is FIRST of the string β followed by a; if β derives ε, then a itself is included. This is the only place lookaheads are created. Do not use FOLLOW(B).

items: For each set I and each grammar symbol X, compute goto(I, X) as the closure of all [A → α X . β, a] such that [A → α . X β, a] is in I.
Add every new set; repeat until no new sets appear.
Record each goto as an edge of the automaton.

blocks.text: For each state i and terminal a, fill ACTION. If [A → α . a β, b] is in I_i and goto(I_i, a)=I_j, set ACTION[i,a] = shift j. If [A → α ., a] is in I_i, set ACTION[i,a] = reduce A→α, unless A = S'. If [S' → S ., $] is in I_i, set ACTION[i,$] = accept. For each nonterminal A, if goto(I_i, A)=I_j, set GOTO[i,A]=j. A blank entry is an error.

Because the reduce action is tied to one lookahead, the table can have fewer conflicts than SLR. The cost is more states: canonical LR(1) does not merge states that differ only in lookaheads. Two states with the same LR(0) core but different lookahead sets are separate. This is why the automaton can be large. The parsing algorithm itself is the same as in Chapter 3.2: use the stack, consult ACTION, shift or reduce, and follow GOTO after a reduce. LALR (Chapter 3.5) merges such states and keeps most of the power.

In the SLR table, the state with [S → L . = R] and [R → L .] reduces R → L on every terminal in FOLLOW(R). For this grammar FOLLOW(R) = {=, $}. The terminal = also calls for a shift, so the state has a shift/reduce conflict on =. In the LR(1) table the same state contains [S → L . = R, $] and [R → L ., $]. The reduce entry is written only under $, not under =. The shift on = and the reduce on $ are different columns, so the conflict is gone. The lookahead narrows the reduce action to the context that actually produced the item. The same lookahead is propagated by closure, so the table entry is not guessed after the fact.

figure.caption: SLR reduces R → L on every token in FOLLOW(R) = {=, $}, which clashes with the shift on =. The LR(1) item carries only the lookahead $, so the reduce moves to the $ column and = is a plain shift.

spec.aria: Two versions of state I2: under SLR the = entry holds both shift 6 and reduce R → L, a conflict; under LR(1) the items carry lookahead $, so = only shifts and the reduce is under $.

examples.question: Grammar: S → L = R | R, L → * R | id, R → L. (a) Compute FIRST and FOLLOW. (b) Show the SLR shift/reduce conflict in the state with S → L . = R and R → L . (c) Give the LR(1) items for that state and the ACTION entries, and count conflicts.
steps: FIRST(L) = {*, id}. FIRST(R) = {*, id}. FIRST(S) = FIRST(L) ∪ FIRST(R) = {*, id}.

FOLLOW(S) = {$}. From S → L = R, = ∈ FOLLOW(L) and $ ∈ FOLLOW(R). From R → L, FOLLOW(R) ⊆ FOLLOW(L), so $ ∈ FOLLOW(L). From L → * R, FOLLOW(L) ⊆ FOLLOW(R), so = ∈ FOLLOW(R). Hence FOLLOW(L) = {=, $} and FOLLOW(R) = {=, $}.

SLR state I2 has items S → L . = R and R → L . . ACTION on = has both shift (to the state with S → L = . R) and reduce R → L because = ∈ FOLLOW(R). ACTION on $ has reduce R → L. So I2 has 1 shift/reduce conflict, on =.

LR(1) closure at the start: [S' → . S, $] adds [S → . L = R, $] and [S → . R, $]. The first adds L items with lookahead =; the second adds [R → . L, $], which adds L items with lookahead $. After goto on L, state I2 contains [S → L . = R, $] and [R → L ., $].
LR(1) ACTION for I2: on = shift to the state with [S → L = . R, $]; on $ reduce R → L. No reduce entry on =. The counts are: |FIRST(S)| = 2, |FOLLOW(L)| = 2, SLR conflicts = 1, LR(1) conflicts = 0.
examples.answer: SLR has 1 shift/reduce conflict on = in state I2; LR(1) has 0 because R → L reduces only on $, so the grammar is LR(1) but not SLR.

traps: Using FOLLOW(A) for reduce lookaheads is SLR, not LR(1). LR(1) uses the lookahead written in the item.
In closure, FIRST(β a) includes a when β can derive ε. Leaving out a loses valid reductions.
The lookahead is not the symbol after the dot. Shift entries use the symbol after the dot; reduce entries use the item's lookahead.
Canonical LR(1) keeps states with the same core and different lookaheads separate. Merging them is LALR.
A state may contain the same production with different lookaheads; their reduce sets must be combined in that state, not treated as a conflict with each other.

quiz.q: Define an LR(1) item [A → α . β, a]. What does each part mean?
quiz.a: A → αβ is a production. The dot shows how much of αβ is matched. a is one terminal lookahead that must follow A when this item is used.

quiz.q: Why can LR(1) remove a shift/reduce conflict that SLR reports?
quiz.a: SLR reduces on all terminals in FOLLOW of the left-hand side. LR(1) reduces only on the item's lookahead. If the shift terminal is not that lookahead, the two actions land in different table columns.

quiz.q: For item [A → α . B β, a] and production B → γ, list the closure items and their lookaheads.
quiz.a: Add [B → . γ, b] for every terminal b in FIRST(β a). If β derives ε, then a is also in FIRST(β a).

quiz.q: In the grammar of the example, give the LR(1) ACTION entries of state I2.
quiz.a: ACTION[I2, =] = shift to the state with [S → L = . R, $]. ACTION[I2, $] = reduce R → L. Other terminals are errors.

quiz.q: Explain why R → L . in I2 has lookahead $ but not =.
quiz.a: It comes from [R → . L, $] in the closure of [S → . R, $]. The closure lookahead is FIRST(ε $) = $, so = is never added for this item.

quiz.q: What is the start item of the canonical LR(1) collection?
Why does canonical LR(1) usually need more states than SLR?
quiz.a: Canonical LR(1) does not merge two states that have the same LR(0) core but different lookahead sets. SLR uses one LR(0) state per core, so it has fewer states.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical parser generators often build LALR or IELR tables instead of full canonical LR(1), because canonical tables can be large. IELR keeps LR(1) power with fewer states. GLR parsers handle ambiguous or nondeterministic grammars by exploring several parses at once. If you search next, try “IELR parsing” and “GLR parsing”.
